title: How should the flow solver reach heat-exchanger Reynolds numbers?
context: HX-1 needs flow at pore Reynolds numbers of about 1–100 (Castro et al. 2019 ran at 29–145; heat exchangers 10–500). The GPU kernel in 19g already solves the full Navier–Stokes equations (its equilibrium keeps the quadratic velocity terms), so no physics is missing: today it simply runs very slowly (lattice speed about 0.01) in a very viscous lattice fluid (relaxation time 1.5), which puts the Reynolds number well below 1. Reaching Re 100 means a faster lattice flow and a much less viscous lattice fluid, and the question is whether the present collision rule (two relaxation times, TRT) holds up there or a new, more stable rule is needed. Either way the creeping-flow path the cards, sweep and Sweep port use stays exactly as it is.

log_refs.entry: §3.1 TRT with magic parameter 3/16; §11.2 HX-1 lattice limits (speed ≤ 0.1, relaxation time clear of ½, Re near 100 at 64³)
§12 check F3: TRT + CLI walls keep permeability to 2 ppm across relaxation times 0.6–2.0

options.name: Same kernel, viscosity set per point
options.summary: Keep D3Q19, TRT and CLI walls. Each Reynolds point keeps the lattice flow at about 0.03 mean pore speed (peaks near 0.1; compressibility error scales with the speed squared, a few tenths of a percent at the mean speed, checked on a straight channel where the exact answer has no inertia at all) and lowers the relaxation time toward 0.51 to reach its Reynolds number. The magic parameter (3/16 now, or 1/4, which is more stable for fast flow) is settled by a GPU bench before coding.

pros: No new kernel: every check already passed (F1–F11, W1–W5) still describes the code that runs.
TRT with CLI walls keeps the wall in place whatever the relaxation time (check F3, 2 ppm), so the answer depends on the Reynolds number alone and changing viscosity per point is safe.

The grid, not stability, is the real ceiling: at 64³ a 70 % gyroid has about 29 cells across its pores, and the boundary layers at Re 100 are already only about 3 cells thick. A more stable rule would mostly buy points the grid cannot resolve.
A console bench on today's main (no code change) can measure stability, steps and time at Re 1–200 before anything is built.
cons: Close to a relaxation time of ½, TRT can go unstable at sharp strut edges; the cap (Re about 100 at 64³, about 400 at 128³) is an estimate until the bench runs.
A less viscous lattice fluid settles more slowly: steps per point grow roughly as one over the viscosity, so the top point costs about 10–40 times what a creeping-flow solve does.
If the bench shows instability below Re 100 at 64³, this option needs the 1/4 parameter or a cap lower than users want.
options.effort: No extra effort beyond HX-1 itself (about 3 sessions in all); half an hour of Matt's time for the GPU bench.

options.name: New, more stable collision rule
options.summary: Replace TRT for inertial runs with a cumulant or regularized collision rule, which stays stable much closer to zero viscosity and is the usual choice for higher-Reynolds lattice Boltzmann work. Creeping flow keeps TRT.
options.sketch: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 180'><line x1='40' y1='150' x2='300' y2='150' stroke='currentColor'/><line x1='40' y1='150' x2='40' y2='20' stroke='currentColor'/><text x='170' y='172' font-size='12' fill='currentColor' text-anchor='middle'>Reynolds number</text><text x='16' y='88' font-size='12' fill='currentColor' text-anchor='middle' transform='rotate(-90 16 88)'>relaxation time</text><path d='M44 30 C120 40 180 112 296 138' fill='none' stroke='var(--accent)' stroke-width='3'/><line x1='40' y1='142' x2='300' y2='142' stroke='var(--good)' stroke-dasharray='5 4'/><text x='52' y='136' font-size='11' fill='var(--good)'>lower floor</text><rect x='230' y='20' width='70' height='130' fill='var(--muted)' opacity='0.25'/><line x1='230' y1='20' x2='230' y2='150' stroke='var(--muted)' stroke-dasharray='3 3'/><text x='236' y='34' font-size='11' fill='currentColor'>unresolved</text></svg>
pros: More headroom against blow-ups at sharp edges and thin throats.
Opens a path to the top of the heat-exchanger range (Re 200–500) on finer grids later.
cons: Two kernels to keep: the GPU step, stress and velocity shaders and the Float64 CPU reference all need a second version, and the wall checks (F1–F7, W1–W4) must be re-run and may fail as Bouzidi walls did with TRT.
The proven property that the wall stays put as viscosity changes is specific to TRT with a fixed magic parameter; a new rule needs its own proof.
Stability past the grid limit buys little accuracy: under-resolved boundary layers give stable but wrong pressure drop.
A new collision operator is a larger change than the request needs, before any measurement says TRT is not enough.
options.effort: About 2 extra sessions on top of HX-1, mostly re-validation.

criteria.name: Physical fidelity
criteria.note: both are full Navier–Stokes; accuracy is set by the grid in both

criteria.name: Run time
criteria.note: settling time is physics, not the collision rule

criteria.name: Credibility to a reviewer
criteria.note: TRT + interpolated walls is the documented porous-media standard (Khirevich et al. 2015)

recommendation: The grid limits accuracy before TRT's stability does, so a new collision rule would mostly buy points the grid cannot resolve. Bench first; move to B only if TRT blows up below Re 100 at 64³.

settles.key: lattice Boltzmann collision for inertial flow
settles.value: D3Q19 TRT with CLI interpolated walls (no new collision operator); Reynolds number reached by lowering the relaxation time per point at a mean pore lattice speed of about 0.03; magic parameter 3/16, or 1/4 if the GPU bench shows it is needed
